name: Engineering management vocabulary
description: The 100 terms a technology leader needs for running teams, delivery and engineering organisations.

cards.subject: retrospective
says: is a regular meeting where a team looks back at how it worked and agrees what to change
focuses on the way of working rather than on the product
cards.use: want a team to improve how it works after a period of work
not: is a meeting that plans the work for the next period

cards.subject: sprint planning
says: is the meeting where a team chooses what it will take on in the next period
turns the top of the backlog into a commitment the team believes it can meet
cards.use: need to agree what the team will work on over the next two weeks
not: is a review of how the team worked in the last period

cards.subject: capacity planning
says: works out how much work a team can take on given its people and their time
allows for leave, meetings and support work
cards.use: need to know how much a team can really deliver next month
not: lists everything the team might ever do

cards.subject: work-in-progress limit
says: caps how many items may be in progress at once
makes a team finish work before it starts more
cards.use: see too many tasks half-done at the same time
not: sets the maximum number of people on a team

cards.subject: Kanban
says: shows work on a board with a column for each stage
pulls new work in only when there is capacity
cards.use: want to see where work is stuck and limit what is started
not: fixes the work for a set period at the start

cards.subject: story point
says: is a relative measure of the effort and complexity of a piece of work
is used by a team to compare items rather than to measure time
cards.use: need a team to size work without promising hours
not: is a fixed number of hours

cards.subject: definition of ready
says: is the checklist an item must meet before a team starts on it
covers things like clear acceptance criteria and known dependencies
cards.use: find that the team keeps starting work that is not well enough understood
not: is the checklist that says work is finished

cards.subject: working agreement
says: is a short set of rules a team agrees for how it works together
covers things such as meeting times and how reviews are done
cards.use: need a team to agree how it will behave day to day
not: is the legal contract between the company and a supplier

cards.subject: team charter
says: states a team's purpose, scope, members and how it makes decisions
is agreed when a team is formed or reshaped
cards.use: are forming a new team and need to state what it is for
not: is a list of the tasks in a sprint

cards.subject: spike
says: is a short, time-boxed piece of work to answer a question or reduce uncertainty
produces knowledge rather than a finished feature
cards.use: need to find out whether an approach is feasible before committing
not: is a feature released to every user at once

cards.subject: structured interview
says: asks every candidate the same questions in the same order
scores answers against agreed criteria
cards.use: want hiring decisions that compare candidates fairly
not: is a free conversation with no set questions

cards.subject: interview scorecard
says: lists the qualities a role needs and a rating scale for each
helps interviewers record evidence against the same criteria
cards.use: need interviewers to rate candidates on the same criteria
not: is the final offer letter

cards.subject: 30-60-90 plan
says: sets out what a new starter will learn and deliver in their first 30, 60 and 90 days
gives a new hire and their manager shared early expectations
cards.use: have a new engineer starting and want clear early goals
not: is a plan for a 90-day project

cards.subject: mentoring
says: pairs a person with a more experienced colleague who shares advice and experience
is led by the person being mentored
cards.use: want a junior to learn from someone who has done the job
not: tells a person exactly what to do and checks that they do it

cards.subject: coaching
says: helps a person work out their own answers through questions
focuses on their goals and how they will reach them
cards.use: want someone to find their own solution rather than be told
not: passes on the coach's own experience as instructions

cards.subject: sponsorship
says: is a senior person using their influence to open opportunities for someone
goes beyond advice by putting that person's name forward
cards.use: want to put a talented person forward for a stretching role
not: is the same as giving career advice over coffee

cards.subject: calibration
says: is a meeting where managers compare their ratings to keep them consistent
guards against one manager rating much more harshly or generously than another
cards.use: need performance ratings to mean the same across teams
not: is a test of how accurate a machine is

cards.subject: promotion packet
says: is the written case for promoting someone, with evidence against the level's expectations
is reviewed by people beyond the person's manager
cards.use: need to make the case that someone is working at the next level
not: is a summary of someone's pay history

cards.subject: talent review
says: is a leadership discussion of the strengths, potential and development of the people in a group
feeds succession planning
cards.use: need leaders to discuss who is ready for bigger roles
not: is a recruitment event for outside candidates

cards.subject: nine-box grid
says: plots people by current performance and potential on a three-by-three grid
is used to guide development and succession discussions
cards.use: want a simple picture of performance against potential across a group
not: is a nine-step hiring process

cards.subject: situation-behaviour-impact feedback
says: describes the situation, the person's behaviour and its impact
keeps feedback specific and about observable actions
cards.use: need to give feedback that is specific rather than a judgement of the person
not: tells a person how they compare with their peers

cards.subject: performance review
says: is a formal assessment of how well someone has done against their goals
usually happens at set points in the year
cards.use: reach the point of the year for a formal assessment
not: is a daily check on whether work is done

cards.subject: objective setting
says: agrees what a person is expected to achieve over a period
links individual work to team and company goals
cards.use: need to agree what someone will deliver this half
not: measures how well someone did last year

cards.subject: underperformance
says: is when someone's work falls below the standard the role needs
should be addressed early, clearly and with support
cards.use: see that someone's work has been below the expected level for weeks
not: is a one-off mistake that was quickly fixed

cards.subject: development plan
says: sets out the skills a person wants to build and how they will build them
is agreed between the person and their manager
cards.use: want to plan how someone will grow over the next year
not: is a plan to build a new product

cards.subject: stretch assignment
says: is a task slightly beyond a person's current level, given to help them grow
comes with support so that they can succeed
cards.use: want to give someone a chance to take on bigger responsibility
not: is extra unpaid work added to a heavy load

cards.subject: recognition
says: tells people that their work was valued
works best when it is specific and timely
cards.use: want people to know that a particular piece of work mattered
not: is a pay rise given once a year

cards.subject: radical candour
says: is giving direct feedback while showing that you care about the person
sits between being harsh and being too nice to be honest
cards.use: want to be honest with someone without damaging the relationship
not: means saying whatever you think with no regard for the person

cards.subject: burnout
says: is exhaustion from prolonged stress that reduces a person's energy and effectiveness
is made more likely by sustained overload and lack of control
cards.use: see a strong engineer becoming withdrawn and tired after months of overload
not: is a short tiredness that goes after a good night's sleep

cards.subject: career conversation
says: is a talk about where a person wants their career to go
looks beyond the current role
cards.use: want to understand what someone hopes to do next
not: is a conversation about this week's tasks

cards.subject: engineering culture
says: is the shared habits and values that shape how engineers work
shows in what is rewarded, tolerated and discussed
cards.use: need to describe how engineers in the organisation really behave
not: is the office layout and perks

cards.subject: blameless culture
says: looks for the causes of failures in systems and decisions rather than in individuals
encourages people to report problems early
cards.use: want people to speak up about mistakes without fear
not: means nobody is ever held accountable for anything

cards.subject: inner source
says: applies open-source ways of working to code shared inside a company
lets teams contribute to each other's code through reviewed changes
cards.use: want teams to improve shared code without waiting for its owners
not: publishes the company's code for the whole world to use

cards.subject: guild
says: is a group of people across teams who share a craft and learn together
has no formal reporting line
cards.use: want people with the same craft in different teams to share practice
not: is a team that owns one product

cards.subject: community of practice
says: is a group of people who share a field and learn from one another
meets regularly to share what works
cards.use: want people who share a profession to learn from each other across the organisation
not: is a group of customers who help each other

cards.subject: documentation culture
says: treats writing things down as part of the work
reduces dependence on what individuals remember
cards.use: see knowledge locked in a few people's heads
not: means writing a long document for every task

cards.subject: RFC process
says: asks an author to write a proposal and invite comments before a major change
records the options considered and the decision taken
cards.use: want a significant change reviewed by the people it affects before work starts
not: is a legal request for payment

cards.subject: design review
says: is a meeting where peers examine a proposed design before it is built
looks for risks and alternatives early
cards.use: want a design challenged before the team builds it
not: is a review of how a built feature looks to users

cards.subject: decision log
says: records important decisions with their date, reasons and owner
lets people see why something was decided
cards.use: want to remember why a choice was made six months ago
not: lists tasks waiting to be done

cards.subject: disagree and commit
says: is accepting a decision after you have argued your case, and then backing it fully
avoids work being held up by endless debate
cards.use: have lost an argument but the team needs to move forward
not: means refusing to take part in a decision you opposed

cards.subject: critical path
says: is the longest chain of dependent tasks in a project
decides the earliest date the project can finish
cards.use: need to know which delays would delay the whole project
not: is the shortest route to deliver a feature

cards.subject: cone of uncertainty
says: shows that estimates are widest at the start of a project and narrow as work proceeds
reminds teams that early estimates carry large error
cards.use: are asked for a firm date for a project that has barely started
not: shows that estimates grow more uncertain as a project nears the end

cards.subject: Brooks's law
says: says that adding people to a late software project makes it later
arises because new people need time to learn and communication grows
cards.use: are tempted to add engineers to a project that is behind
not: says a team should always grow as a project progresses

cards.subject: release train
says: ships on a fixed timetable, with whatever is ready going out on each departure
makes delivery predictable by fixing the date rather than the content
cards.use: want regular, predictable releases
not: delays every release until all planned features are finished

cards.subject: code freeze
says: is a period when no new changes are merged, apart from urgent fixes
is used to stabilise a release or protect a busy period
cards.use: need to protect a release or a peak trading period from late changes
not: is the deletion of old code

cards.subject: release management
says: plans, coordinates and controls how software is released
covers scheduling, approvals and communication
cards.use: need someone to coordinate what goes live and when
not: is the writing of the code that is released

cards.subject: scope creep
says: is the gradual growth of what a project must deliver without matching time or budget
comes from many small additions that each seem harmless
cards.use: see requests being added to a project one by one
not: is a project finishing earlier than planned

cards.subject: burn-up chart
says: plots completed work against the total scope over time
shows both progress and changes in scope
cards.use: want to see how much is done and how much the scope has grown
not: shows only the work remaining, falling to zero

cards.subject: throughput forecasting
says: predicts delivery dates from how many items a team has finished in past periods
uses real history instead of estimates for each item
cards.use: want a forecast based on what the team has actually delivered
not: adds up the estimates for every item

cards.subject: dependency mapping
says: shows which teams and systems a piece of work relies on
helps spot delays and conflicts before they happen
cards.use: need to see which other teams could block a project
not: lists the libraries imported by one program

cards.subject: service level indicator
says: is a measurement of how a service is performing, such as the share of successful requests
is what a service level objective is checked against
cards.use: need a number that shows how well a service is working
not: is the target that the service promises to meet

cards.subject: error budget
says: is the amount of unreliability a service may have before it breaks its objective
lets a team balance new features against stability
cards.use: need to decide whether the team can keep releasing or must fix reliability
not: is the money set aside for fixing bugs

cards.subject: incident commander
says: is the person who leads the response to a live incident
coordinates people and decisions rather than fixing the fault personally
cards.use: need one person to coordinate the response to a major outage
not: is the engineer who fixes the fault

cards.subject: on-call fatigue
says: is the exhaustion from frequent out-of-hours alerts and interrupted sleep
leads to mistakes and to people leaving
cards.use: see on-call engineers worn out by constant pages
not: is the tiredness after a long meeting

cards.subject: runbook
says: is a documented set of steps for handling a known operational task or alert
lets a tired engineer follow a proven procedure
cards.use: need steps to follow when a particular alert fires
not: is a plan for the whole year's releases

cards.subject: toil
says: is repetitive manual operational work that could be automated and grows with the service
produces no lasting improvement
cards.use: see engineers spending their time on routine manual tasks
not: is skilled design work that improves the system

cards.subject: chaos engineering
says: deliberately injects failures into a system to see how it copes
aims to find weaknesses before real outages do
cards.use: want to test whether the system survives the loss of a component
not: means working without any planning

cards.subject: reliability review
says: is a regular look at how a service has performed against its objectives
decides where to invest to make it more dependable
cards.use: need to decide what reliability work to do next quarter
not: is a performance appraisal of the on-call team

cards.subject: production readiness review
says: checks that a service is ready to run in production before launch
covers monitoring, runbooks, capacity and recovery
cards.use: need to confirm that a new service can be safely operated before it goes live
not: is a test that the interface looks finished

cards.subject: incident severity level
says: classifies an incident by how much harm it does
decides how fast people must respond and who is told
cards.use: need to decide how urgently to respond to a fault
not: is the number of people affected over a year

cards.subject: SPACE framework
says: measures developer productivity across satisfaction, performance, activity, communication and efficiency
warns against judging productivity by a single number
cards.use: need a balanced way to think about how productive engineers are
not: counts the lines of code written each week

cards.subject: developer experience
says: is how easy and pleasant it is for engineers to do their work
covers tools, builds, documentation and processes
cards.use: see engineers slowed by poor tools and slow builds
not: is the number of years an engineer has worked

cards.subject: cognitive load
says: is the amount of mental effort a person must hold to do their work
grows when a team owns too many things
cards.use: see a team struggling because it is responsible for too much
not: is how many tasks a computer can run at once

cards.subject: flow efficiency
says: is the share of a work item's elapsed time in which it is actually being worked on
is low when items spend most of their time waiting
cards.use: want to know how much of a delivery's time is spent waiting
not: is how many hours an engineer works per day

cards.subject: rework rate
says: is the share of work that has to be redone or fixed after it was thought finished
signals problems with quality or unclear requirements
cards.use: see a lot of finished work coming back to be fixed
not: is the speed at which new work is started

cards.subject: escaped defect
says: is a bug found by users after release rather than by the team before it
shows what testing missed
cards.use: need to count bugs that reached customers
not: is a bug found and fixed during development

cards.subject: leading indicator
says: is a measure that changes before the outcome you care about
gives an early warning that a result is likely to move
cards.use: want an early signal that delivery is about to slip
not: is a measure that reports what has already happened

cards.subject: lagging indicator
says: is a measure that reports an outcome after it has happened
confirms results but arrives too late to change them
cards.use: need to report last quarter's results
not: is a measure that changes before the outcome

cards.subject: guardrail metric
says: is a measure that must not get worse while a team pursues a goal
protects against gaining one result at the cost of another
cards.use: want to make sure a push for speed does not harm quality
not: is the main target the team is trying to hit

cards.subject: vanity metric
says: is a number that looks impressive but does not guide decisions
goes up whatever the team does
cards.use: see a chart that looks good but tells you nothing to act on
not: is a measure tied directly to a decision

cards.subject: matrix organisation
says: has people report to a functional manager while working on projects led by others
creates two lines of accountability
cards.use: see an engineer who reports to one manager but takes direction from a project lead
not: has every person report to exactly one boss with no project work

cards.subject: product trio
says: is a product manager, a designer and an engineer who make product decisions together
keeps discovery work close to delivery
cards.use: want product decisions made with design and engineering input from the start
not: is a group of three executives

cards.subject: dual-track agile
says: runs discovery of what to build alongside delivery of what is already decided
keeps a team from building unvalidated ideas
cards.use: want to test ideas with users while the team keeps delivering
not: means two teams doing exactly the same work

cards.subject: stakeholder map
says: shows who is affected by or can influence a project and how much
helps decide how to engage each person
cards.use: need to see who must be kept informed or consulted
not: is a diagram of a computer network

cards.subject: service catalogue
says: lists the services a team or function offers and how to request them
makes clear what is on offer and what it costs
cards.use: want other teams to know what your team provides and how to ask
not: is a list of customers

cards.subject: internal customer
says: is a colleague or team that uses what another team provides
should be treated with the care given to a paying customer
cards.use: need to think of another department as the people you serve
not: is a paying member of the public

cards.subject: shared service
says: is a function, such as IT support, provided once and used by many parts of the organisation
aims for consistency and lower cost
cards.use: need one team to provide something that many parts of the business use
not: is a service that each department builds for itself

cards.subject: centre of excellence
says: is a team that holds deep expertise and spreads good practice
advises other teams rather than doing all the work itself
cards.use: want a group that sets standards and helps others adopt them
not: is the company's head office building

cards.subject: operating cadence
says: is the regular rhythm of meetings and reviews that runs an organisation
makes planning, reporting and decisions predictable
cards.use: want a predictable rhythm of planning and review across teams
not: is the speed of a team's typing

cards.subject: team API
says: is how a team expects other teams to work with it, such as its services, documentation and requests
reduces unplanned interruptions
cards.use: want other teams to know how to work with yours without ad hoc interruptions
not: is a programming interface exposed by a web service

cards.subject: run versus change
says: separates the cost of keeping systems running from the cost of changing them
shows how much of the budget is left for new work
cards.use: need to show how much spend goes on maintenance rather than new development
not: separates cloud costs from office costs

cards.subject: fully loaded cost
says: is the total cost of employing someone, including salary, benefits, tax and overheads
is higher than their pay alone
cards.use: need to know what an engineer really costs the company
not: is the salary on their contract

cards.subject: contractor
says: is someone engaged for a period or a project and paid by the day or hour
is usually not an employee and has different rights
cards.use: need extra capacity for a defined project without hiring
not: is a permanent employee on the payroll

cards.subject: capacity versus demand
says: compares how much work a team can do with how much is being asked of it
shows where the team is overloaded
cards.use: need to show leaders that requests exceed what the team can deliver
not: compares last year's budget with this year's

cards.subject: vendor scorecard
says: rates a supplier against agreed measures such as quality, delivery and responsiveness
gives evidence for contract reviews
cards.use: need to judge how well a supplier is performing over time
not: is a supplier's price list

cards.subject: cloud commitment
says: is an agreement to spend a set amount with a cloud provider in return for a lower rate
carries a risk of paying for capacity that is not used
cards.use: want a cheaper cloud rate in exchange for committing to spend
not: is a promise to move every system to the cloud

cards.subject: unit cost
says: is the cost to deliver one unit of something, such as one transaction or one customer
shows whether efficiency is improving as volume grows
cards.use: want to know the cost of serving one more user
not: is the total cost of a department

cards.subject: showback
says: reports to each team what its technology use costs, without charging it
raises awareness of cost
cards.use: want teams to see what they spend without moving money between budgets
not: moves money from each team's budget to the central one

cards.subject: chargeback
says: bills each team for the technology it uses, moving money between budgets
makes teams directly accountable for what they consume
cards.use: want teams to pay for what they use out of their own budgets
not: reports costs without moving any money

cards.subject: cost allocation tag
says: is a label attached to a cloud resource to show which team or product owns its cost
makes it possible to split a shared bill
cards.use: need to work out which team is responsible for each cloud cost
not: is a security label for sensitive data

cards.subject: golden path
says: is the recommended, well-supported way to build and run something in the organisation
makes the right thing the easy thing
cards.use: want teams to choose a supported default rather than invent their own
not: is a mandatory process that no team may depart from for any reason

cards.subject: paved road
says: is a set of supported tools and platforms that teams are encouraged to use
reduces the need for each team to solve the same problem
cards.use: want to offer a well-supported route that most teams will choose
not: is a rule that forbids using any other tool

cards.subject: technology standard
says: is an agreed choice or rule for how technology is used across the organisation
keeps systems consistent and supportable
cards.use: need everyone to use the same approach to a common problem
not: is a suggestion that nobody has to follow

cards.subject: exception process
says: lets a team ask to depart from a standard, with reasons and approval
keeps departures visible and time-limited
cards.use: need a team to be allowed to depart from a standard with agreement
not: removes the standard for everyone

cards.subject: deprecation policy
says: sets how and when something will be retired, with warning to its users
gives users time to move
cards.use: need to retire an old service without surprising its users
not: deletes a feature with no notice

cards.subject: end of life
says: is the date after which a product or version is no longer supported
means no more fixes, including security fixes
cards.use: find that software your system runs on will stop receiving security updates
not: is the date a product is first released

cards.subject: open source policy
says: sets rules for using and contributing to open-source software
covers licences, security and who may approve use
cards.use: need rules on which open-source components teams may use
not: is a rule that all code must be published openly

cards.subject: architecture principle
says: is a short statement of a rule that guides design decisions
is chosen to reflect what the organisation values
cards.use: need to guide many teams towards consistent design choices
not: is a diagram of a particular system

cards.subject: technical design authority
says: is a group that reviews and approves significant technical decisions
balances team freedom with consistency
cards.use: need a body that approves major technical choices across teams
not: is the supplier that wrote the system

cards.subject: technology adoption curve
says: describes how a new technology spreads from early adopters to the majority
shows when a technology is proven enough for wider use
cards.use: need to judge whether a new technology is mature enough to adopt
not: is a graph of a company's revenue over time

qa.q: Which meeting looks back at how a team worked and agrees what to change?
qa.why: A retrospective reviews the way of working.

qa.q: Which meeting decides what the team will take on in the next two weeks?
qa.why: Sprint planning chooses the next period's work.

qa.q: A team has too many tasks half-done at once. What helps?
qa.why: A limit makes the team finish before starting more.

qa.q: What are story points?
qa.right: A relative measure of effort and complexity, not a number of hours
wrong: A fixed number of hours per task
A score for how happy the team is
qa.why: Points compare items rather than promise time.

qa.q: A client keeps adding small requests to a project one by one. What is this?
qa.why: Scope grows without matching time or budget.

qa.q: A junior engineer wants advice from someone who has done the job. What fits?
qa.why: Mentoring shares experience and advice.

qa.q: You want to compare candidates fairly. Which interview approach helps?
qa.right: A structured interview with the same questions for everyone
wrong: Asking each candidate a different question
qa.why: Structured interviews score answers against agreed criteria.

qa.q: An alert fires at 3am and the on-call engineer is not sure what to do. What helps most?
qa.right: A runbook with the steps for that alert
qa.why: A runbook documents a proven procedure.

qa.q: Which feedback is specific and about behaviour?
qa.right: I noticed that in Tuesday's review you interrupted Sam three times, and it meant the team stopped sharing ideas
wrong: You are not a team player
qa.why: Situation, behaviour and impact keep feedback specific.

qa.q: You need to see who must be kept informed about a project. What do you draw up?
qa.why: A stakeholder map shows who is affected or can influence.

qa.q: A task on the critical path slips by a week. What is the likely effect?
qa.right: The project finishes a week later unless time is made up elsewhere
wrong: Nothing, as the other tasks are unaffected
The project finishes a week earlier
The task is dropped from the plan
qa.why: The critical path decides the finish date.

qa.q: A late project looks set to miss its date and a manager wants to add five engineers. Which law warns against this?
qa.why: Adding people to a late project can make it later.

qa.q: Which chart shows both progress and growth in scope?
wrong: A burn-down chart that shows only remaining work
qa.why: A burn-up plots completed work against total scope.

qa.q: The team needs a short piece of work to find out whether an approach is feasible. What is it?
qa.why: A spike answers a question rather than delivering a feature.

qa.q: After an outage, how does a blameless culture approach the review?
qa.right: It looks for causes in systems and decisions, not individuals
wrong: It names the engineer who caused it
It decides who should be disciplined
qa.why: Blameless reviews find system causes and encourage reporting.

qa.q: Engineers spend each week restarting the same servers by hand. What is this called?
qa.why: Toil is repetitive manual work that could be automated.

qa.q: Who coordinates the response to a major live incident?
qa.why: The commander leads the response rather than fixing the fault.

qa.q: Which is a leading indicator that delivery may slip?
qa.right: Pull requests waiting longer and longer for review
wrong: The number of bugs fixed last year
The total lines of code written
qa.why: A leading indicator changes before the outcome.

qa.q: What does an engineer really cost the company?
qa.right: Their salary plus benefits, tax and overheads
wrong: Only the salary on the contract
qa.why: Fully loaded cost is higher than pay alone.

qa.q: A database version your system runs on stops receiving security updates next month. What has been reached?
qa.why: After end of life there are no more fixes.

qa.q: An engineer's work has been below the expected standard for several weeks. What should you do first?
qa.right: Talk to them early and clearly, and offer support
wrong: Tell the rest of the team
Move their tasks to someone else without telling them
qa.why: Underperformance should be addressed early, clearly and with support.

qa.q: A strong engineer has become withdrawn and tired after months of overload. What is the likely problem, and what helps?
qa.right: Burnout; reduce the load and talk to them
wrong: A skills gap; send them on a course
qa.why: Sustained overload leads to burnout.

qa.q: Before building a major feature, you want peers to challenge the design. What do you hold?
qa.why: A design review examines a design before it is built.

qa.q: A service has used up its error budget. What should the team do?
qa.right: Slow feature releases and focus on reliability
wrong: Release faster to make up for it
Ignore the budget until next year
qa.why: An exhausted error budget shifts work to stability.

qa.q: A CEO asks for an exact date at the very start of a large project. Which idea explains why that is unreliable?
qa.why: Early estimates carry the widest error.

qa.q: Releases leave on a fixed timetable with whatever is ready. What is this?
qa.why: A release train fixes the date, not the content.

qa.q: A senior leader uses their influence to put a talented engineer forward for a leadership role. What is this?
qa.why: Sponsorship opens opportunities, not only advice.

qa.q: Managers meet to make sure ratings mean the same across teams. What is this?
qa.why: Calibration keeps ratings consistent.

qa.q: A leader wants to judge engineers by commits per week. Why is that a weak measure?
qa.right: One activity measure ignores quality, satisfaction and collaboration
qa.why: The SPACE framework warns against a single number.

qa.q: A team is pushing for faster releases. Which measure should it watch to make sure quality does not suffer?
qa.why: A guardrail must not get worse while pursuing a goal.

qa.q: A team owns twelve services and keeps missing its work. Which concept describes the problem?
qa.why: Too much to hold in mind slows a team.

qa.q: You want teams to choose a well-supported default rather than invent their own. What do you provide?
qa.why: A golden path makes the right thing the easy thing.

qa.q: Committing to spend a set amount with a cloud provider for a lower rate carries what risk?
qa.right: Paying for capacity that goes unused
wrong: Having to move everything to the cloud
Losing the right to cancel any service
qa.why: A commitment is paid whether or not it is used.

qa.q: Teams are told what their technology costs but are not charged for it. What is this?
qa.why: Showback reports cost without moving money.

qa.q: A significant change should be reviewed by the people it affects before work starts. Which process fits?
qa.why: An RFC invites comment before the change.

qa.q: You lost the argument but the team needs to move on. What do you do?
qa.right: Disagree and commit: back the decision fully
qa.why: It avoids endless debate.

qa.q: A team needs to depart from a technology standard with agreement. Which process lets it?
qa.why: An exception is requested with reasons and approval.

qa.q: You want to find weaknesses by deliberately injecting failures into a system. What is this?
qa.why: It tests how the system copes with failure.

qa.q: A new service is about to launch. Which review confirms it can be safely operated?
qa.why: It checks monitoring, runbooks, capacity and recovery.

qa.q: Teams want to improve a shared library without waiting for its owners. Which approach fits?
wrong: Open-sourcing the code to the public
qa.why: Inner source uses open-source habits inside the company.

qa.q: Each team is billed for the technology it uses, with money moving between budgets. What is this?
qa.why: Chargeback moves money; showback only reports.

qa.q: Leaders plot people by performance and potential on a three-by-three grid. What is it?
qa.why: It guides development and succession discussions.

qa.q: A body approves significant technical decisions across teams, balancing freedom and consistency. What is it?
qa.why: It reviews and approves major technical choices.

qa.q: You want other teams to know how to work with yours without ad hoc interruptions. What do you define?
qa.why: A team API sets expectations for working with a team.

qa.q: You need to judge whether a new technology is proven enough for wider use. Which idea helps?
qa.why: It shows how a technology spreads towards the majority.

termBank.name: Engineering management
termBank.description: Running teams, delivery and engineering organisations: from engineering manager to CTO.
